Loathsome
LOTHE-sum
adj.
From loathe, Saxon lathian, to hate, to be hateful, and the suffix -some. Webster 1828: causing an aversion; exciting disgust; odious. Scripture uses it of a disease, of a wicked man, and of a food God gave in anger.

Biblical Definition

Loathsome means disgusting, and Scripture uses it of things that repel by their own nature. David uses it of his body under God’s hand in a penitential psalm: For my loins are filled with a loathsome disease: and there is no soundness in my flesh (Psalm 38:7). Proverbs uses it of a character: A righteous man hateth lying: but a wicked man is loathsome, and cometh to shame (Proverbs 13:5) — the contrast is exact, one man hates the lie and the other becomes the thing hated. And Numbers uses it in one of the most sobering judgments in Scripture, where God gives His people precisely what they demanded until they cannot stand it: Israel wept for flesh, and God sent quails until it come out at your nostrils, and it be loathsome unto you: because that ye have despised the LORD which is among you (Numbers 11:20). The psalmist summarises that episode in a line every believer should keep: he gave them their request; but sent leanness into their soul (Psalm 106:15). What a man insists on getting can become the punishment for having insisted.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 defines LOATHSOME as causing an aversion; exciting disgust or extreme dislike; odious; and, of food or disease, offensive to the natural feeling.

expand to see more

LOATHSOME, a. — Causing an aversion; exciting disgust; offensive to the taste or the natural feeling.

Odious; hateful; exciting extreme dislike or abhorrence.

LOATHE, v.t. — To feel disgust at; to have an extreme aversion of the appetite to.

Applied in Scripture to a disease, to a wicked character, and to food given in judgment.

From Saxon lathian, to hate — the root also of loath, unwilling, and loathing.

Key Scripture

Psalm 38:7 — "For my loins are filled with a loathsome disease: and there is no soundness in my flesh."

Proverbs 13:5 — "A righteous man hateth lying: but a wicked man is loathsome, and cometh to shame."

Psalm 38:5 — "My wounds stink and are corrupt because of my foolishness."

Isaiah 14:19 — "But thou art cast out of thy grave like an abominable branch, and as the raiment of those that are slain, thrust through with a sword, that go down to the stones of the pit; as a carcase trodden under feet."

Modern Corruption

Numbers 11 records God granting a demand as a judgment, which is the answer to the assumption that a prayer answered in the affirmative is by that fact a prayer God approved.

expand to see more

Israel wept through the whole camp for flesh, remembering the fish, cucumbers, melons, leeks, onions and garlick of Egypt and despising the manna. God’s reply was to send quails for a whole month, until it come out at your nostrils, and it be loathsome unto you, and He gave the reason: because that ye have despised the LORD which is among you. The plague fell while the meat was still between their teeth, and the place was named the graves of lust. Psalm 106:15 puts it in one clause: he gave them their request; but sent leanness into their soul. This is the necessary corrective to any teaching that measures God’s favour by whether He grants what is asked. Getting what one insisted on is sometimes the judgment, and Romans 1 describes the same divine act three times as God gave them up.

Proverbs 13:5 makes a distinction worth holding onto in an age that dislikes the word loathsome applied to any person. The verse does not say a wicked man is disliked; it says he becomes loathsome and comes to shame — the character makes itself repellent by what it does, and shame is its natural end. Scripture is not squeamish about the description, and it is equally unsqueamish about the remedy: David, in Psalm 38, uses the same vocabulary of himself — loathsome disease, stinking wounds, his own foolishness — and ends the psalm not in despair but in petition: Forsake me not, O LORD: O my God, be not far from me. The man who can call his own condition loathsome and still pray has understood both halves of the gospel.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew zara (H2214), loathsome, nauseating; baash (H887), to stink, to become odious; qalah (H7043), to be light, to be despised; Greek bdelusso (G948), to abhor.

expand to see more

Hebrew zara (H2214) — loathsome, nauseating; until it be loathsome unto you (Numbers 11:20).

Hebrew niqleh — from qalah (H7043), to be lightly esteemed, contemptible; a wicked man is loathsome (Proverbs 13:5).

Hebrew baash (H887) — to stink, to become odious; the companion image in Psalm 38:5.

Greek bdelusso (G948) — to abhor, to detest; the root of bdelugma, the abomination of desolation.

Hebrew razon (H7332) — leanness, wasting; sent leanness into their soul (Psalm 106:15).

Usage

"My loins are filled with a loathsome disease (Psalm 38:7) — a man describing his own condition without flinching."

"A wicked man is loathsome, and cometh to shame (Proverbs 13:5) — a character that makes itself repellent."

"Until it be loathsome unto you (Numbers 11:20) — a demand granted, and the granting was the judgment."
